title: Severe background noise narrows the audiovisual temporal binding window without reliably shifting subjective simultaneity
excerpt:
Temporal coherence contributes to audiovisual speech perception, but how competing background noise affects perceived audiovisual synchrony remains unclear. This study examined whether signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) influences the width and midpoint of the perceived-synchrony interval during continuous audiovisual speech perception. Twenty-five adults with normal hearing and normal or corrected-to-normal vision were presented with Harvard/IEEE sentences spoken by a female talker and accompanied by eight-talker babble at −10, 0, and +10 dB SNR.

Using a self-adjustment procedure, participants shifted the relative timing of the auditory and visual streams from audio-leading and visual-leading starting positions until the stimuli were perceived as synchronous. The difference between the resulting audio-leading and visual-leading adjustment endpoints defined the adjustment-derived temporal binding window (TBW), and their midpoint defined the point of subjective simultaneity (PSS).

Results showed that the adjustment-derived TBW was significantly narrower at −10 dB SNR than at 0 or +10 dB SNR, whereas no significant difference was observed between the two higher SNR conditions. PSS did not differ significantly across SNR conditions. These findings suggest that adverse background noise can selectively constrain the temporal range over which audiovisual speech is perceived as simultaneous without producing a reliable shift in the temporal center of perceived simultaneity…
